title: London Customs Accounts, 1380-1560: machine-readable data and research tools
description:
Machine-readable data and browser-based research tools for the particular customs accounts of the port of London, 1380-1560, produced by the project Unlocking Upcycled Medieval Data: North Sea Networks, People, and Commodities in the London Customs Accounts 1380-1560 (Institute of Historical Research, University of London, and Otto-Friedrich-Universität Bamberg).

The London particular customs accounts are the largest surviving serial collection of medieval trade documents in Europe. This dataset "upcycles" existing scholarly transcripts of those accounts — semi-structured text prepared over decades for human readers — into structured, linkable data: 33,742 ladings across 46 account-book files (Volumes I-IV), holding 215,810 cargos; a curated glossary of 2,455 commodity concepts, attested by 19,634 spellings and aligned to Getty AAT and Wikidata; and 267,408 person mentions grouped for identity matching across 40,401 surname and 6,120 forename spellings.

Contributions. Justin Colson and Werner Scheltjens conceived the project and secured its funding, and direct it as co-investigators. Stephen Gadd designed and built the data pipeline, the reconciliation and annotation tools, and the published site. Eliot Benbow and María Grove-Gordillo carried out the historical and linguistic curation: commodity glossary curation, and expert annotation of the cargo entries, including the independent double annotation from which the project's inter-annotator agreement is measured.

Rights. Licensing differs by component. Site code (JavaScript, HTML, CSS) is MIT; project-authored data is CC BY 4.0; Stuart Jenks's transcriptions of the London customs accounts and the Tudor books of rates, as reproduced in the datasets, and all data derived from them are CC BY 4.0, granted by Stuart Jenks on 3 October 2026 (attribute as: "Derived from Stuart Jenks's transcriptions of the London customs accounts and the Tudor books of rates. Licensed CC BY 4.0."); material deriving from other earlier editions and reference works is released only as its rights position is cleared. Each file is published with its rights position stated, and that statement governs where it differs from the single licence recorded here.
notes:
This version archives the project's published data and site: the 46 per-file lading datasets with their annotations, the cargo records, the commodity glossary and the person index, together with the site code and documentation. The figures in the description were measured from this data on 5 October 2026.

Rights. On 3 October 2026 Stuart Jenks granted a CC BY 4.0 licence on his transcriptions, as reproduced in these datasets, and on all data derived from them. Attribute that material as: "Derived from Stuart Jenks's transcriptions of the London customs accounts and the Tudor books of rates. Licensed CC BY 4.0." Site code is MIT. The README ("Status and licence") gives the position component by component.

The data continues to be curated and changes between versions. Cite the version you used; the concept DOI always resolves to the most recent one. Version 0.0.0-beta carried citation metadata only, and no data.
